prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its physiological actions, which enabled receptor-agonist treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: B031 has the clearest chain from physiology to patient benefit on the list: proglucagon processing, identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) amide, its insulinotropic and appetite-related actions, and then a drug class with independently confirmed effects on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. Five of six of us ranked it first, which is not merit in itself, but the independent opening assessments converge on the same reasons: originality, mechanistic clarity, breadth and maturity. A single-achievement prize with Holst, Drucker and Mojsov keeps the award on discovery of the hormone and its biology, in the classic physiology-or-medicine sense, and fits the three-laureate limit.
statement.case_against: The attribution is genuinely contested. Mojsov's priority relative to the Habener group is disputed and Habener is not among the credited names. Knudsen's long-acting analogue design is arguably what turned the biology into a medicine, so a prize limited to the academic trio can be read as under-crediting translation, while adding her forces out one of the three. If the committee cannot defend the credit split, a cleaner and more compact alternative such as the unfolded protein response (Mori, Walter) is the fall-back, though its disease impact is narrower and its therapeutic translation is early.

responses.point: Ranks TNF blockade (Feldmann, Maini) first as a clean two-person bench-to-bedside discovery, and prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen for GLP-1, omitting Mojsov.
responses.response: I agree that TNF is a clean and mature case and that the Feldmann-Maini pairing is compact, and I ranked it sixth mainly because the antibody-engineering and cytokine-cloning credit sits outside the supplied names, not because the impact is smaller. I part from you on GLP-1 attribution. Dropping Mojsov in favour of Knudsen moves the prize toward drug development and leaves out the identification of the active peptide form, which the later biology rests on. I would not make that substitution unless the committee settles that the prize should reward the drug-development track, and I do not think the evidence yet supports that.

responses.point: Argues that optogenetics (Deisseroth, Hegemann, Nagel) is a very original, broadly enabling method and a strong second choice after GLP-1.
responses.response: The originality and breadth are not in doubt, and I ranked it fourth with a different trio that includes Miesenböck. My reservation is attribution. Six names are credited, and any three omit Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck, which is a fairness problem you and Per both acknowledge. It is also a tool rather than a mechanism of physiology or disease, so I would hold it as an alternative rather than put it into a combined prize with GLP-1 and widen the dispute.

responses.point: Ranks CAR-T second and sees GLP-1 and CAR-T as the two largest clinical advances, with the Eshhar and Kuwana gaps unresolved.
responses.response: I agree that CAR-T is a strong candidate and that the clinical durability is real. My concern is that the credit gap is wider than for GLP-1: the first-generation chimeric receptor concept sits outside the credited names, so a Sadelain-June-Rosenberg trio risks crediting translation over conception. I would not pair it with GLP-1 in a two-part prize just to reach a combined clinical headline. It remains a serious alternative if the record on Eshhar can be settled.

responses.point: Places GLP-1 first on the basis of physiology plus peptide chemistry, treats Knudsen as an alternative third slot, and notes a compromise optogenetics trio leaves out three credible names.
responses.response: I share your view that the academic core is Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, and your point that Knudsen's role is largely industrial design is the one I would keep in front of the committee. Where I would press is on whether leaving her out is defensible once the discussion gets to the final ballot, since the citation would then have to be written around discovery of the hormone and its actions rather than the drugs. I wrote it that way deliberately.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the Mojsov versus Habener priority question as settled enough to credit Mojsov without Habener.
Whether the prize should reward the physiology of GLP-1 only or also the development of long-acting analogues, which determines whether Knudsen displaces one of the three.
Whether a two-part configuration would be better than a single GLP-1 prize, given the three-person limit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. My documented connections (spatial transcriptomics co-authorship, single-cell work, co-authors including Rickard Sandberg) concern fields outside the shortlisted ballots.
